title: Frozen Quotas and Contested Numbers: The Political Economy of Transboundary Water Cooperation in Central Asia
content: Transboundary water cooperation in Central Asia is usually framed as a contest over volumes between upstream hydropower and downstream irrigation. This article argues that the more consequential politics lie in three arenas: interstate bargaining over rigid allocations, domestic political economies that constrain credible commitments, and contestation over the authority of hydrological information. Combining process tracing of agreements and protocols from 1992 to 2026 with indicators derived from published Interstate Commission for Water Coordination records for the Syr Darya, we show that approved growing-season limits varied by 0.8% between 2017 and 2024 while upper-basin inflow varied by 21.7%; that unused allocation fell disproportionately on the smaller riparians, with mean burden-sharing indices of 1.31–1.67 for Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan against 0.88 for Uzbekistan; and that only 12 of 30 published inflow forecast ranges contained observed flows. We interpret these patterns as evidence of politically frozen quotas, uneven scarcity burdens and contestable numbers. Seasonal electricity-for-water protocols, the trilateral Kambarata-1 joint venture and Afghanistan’s Qosh Tepa Canal signal a shift from treaty-based to protocol- and asset-based cooperation. We propose a sequenced policy agenda that couples benefit sharing with jointly verified data, due-process enforcement against informal abstraction and a technical track with Afghanistan.
